There's some confusion why earth.nullschool.net does not show the same maximum windspeed for Irma as reported by the National Hurricane Center or local meteorologists. This is true. And knowing why will help you understand the benefits and limitations of the tool.

This post has two images. The first is a zoomed-up image of Irma's eye as forecast for September 10th, 2017, 5 AM EDT. The colors look fairly smooth and you can see the circular shape of the eye. You can also see white dots in a 0.5° lat/lon grid pattern. (Click the "grid" button in the menu to turn them on.) These dots represent the location of the underlying data points as produced by the GFS weather model.

The second image uses exactly the same data, but the colors are blocky. The only difference between these images is that the first uses bilinear interpolation to create those smooth colors whereas the second does not. The wind speeds at the white dots are identical in both images.

Take a closer look at that second image. Each dot--each data point--represents the average wind speed over a large rectangular area. In this case, because it's a 0.5° grid, that area is roughly 1150 square miles, a huge area. As a result, this grid is not fine-grained enough to "see" the fastest winds around the eye of a hurricane because they get averaged out by the very large 0.5° grid cells.

This is the main reason why the wind speeds on earth.nullschool.net are lower than measured by actual planes flying through the hurricane. In most cases, the average wind speed on a 0.5° grid is perfectly fine for representing common weather conditions. But in the extreme conditions near the eyes of hurricanes, the size of the grid becomes critical in being able to resolve the fine-grained details. Too coarse and the accuracy goes down.

So why not use a higher resolution grid? The GFS is actually available on a 0.25° grid as well, which can be viewed when "HD" mode is enabled from the earth menu. (And even then, 0.25° is still too coarse.) But the more fine-grained the grid is, the larger the data becomes. It's a tradeoff between speed/size and accuracy.

As always, consult with multiple authoritative sources: the National Hurricane Center, your local meteorologists, etc. earth.nullschool.net is just a one tool out of many and never replaces actual professionals.
